newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agriculture faces hosts of trade issues next year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agriculture faces hosts of trade issues next year.

text.p: With the fight to revamp U.S. agricultural policy won this year, farmers face a host of challenges on the trade front in 1997, ranging from European concerns over genetically altered crops to Chinese fears of allegedly infected American wheat.
"It's going to be a fun year. ... Nobody's going to get bored," said a high-ranking grain industry official.

Unprecedented increases in crop production outside the United States this year will create stiff competition for U.S. farmers abroad, but agricultural specialists said the landmark new farm bill passed by Congress last April will unleash American producers to better compete in world markets.
The "Freedom to Farm" bill threw out 60 years of U.S. farm policy by removing most federal limits on what farmers grow.

"Freedom to Farm has really positioned the United States very well to take advantage of the opportunities in the world market," said Dan Pearson, policy analyst for Cargill Inc., one of the world's oldest and largest agribusiness companies.
But industry sources said the key in 1997 for agriculture will be how much the Clinton administration fights to open foreign markets for U.S. farmers and to tear down trade barriers.
"Central to the year ahead is how high a priority does the U.S. government place on agriculture," said Pearson.
Pearson and others said U.S. policy makers need to recognise the benefits that liberalising farm trade have for other U.S. industries.

"We have to do a better job of raising agriculture's profile," said an agricultural trade specialist. "If you liberalise (farm) trade, you raise the income of farmers, lower food prices for consumers and boost everyone's income. And then you'd sell more cell phones to those people."
"The Agriculture Department is working in a crisis response mode (on trade issues)," said an industry official. "They need to start looking at issues more pro-actively (in advance)."
At the top of everyone's wish list of things they would like to see go away next year are the fights popping up around the world over import barriers erected due to health concerns.

Rules approved in the last days of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade require that health regulations for agricultural imports cannot be used as disguised trade barriers but must be based on scientific findings.
The World Trade Organisation inherited these new rules, but many officials have said the new organisation was not prepared to deal with the number and scope of alleged violations.

A bitter dispute between China and the United States over U.S. wheat shipments demonstrates how serious such a fight can become. China earlier this year cancelled all purchases of U.S. wheat, claiming it was infected with a fungus called tilletia controversa kuhn, or TCK smut.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman has warned repeatedly that China's stance in the wheat dispute could affect its efforts to be accepted into the World Trade Organisation.

In a recent interview, Glickman rated the China wheat issue as one of the most serious in 1997. "China needs to understand this is a very significant factor in being included in the community of nations in terms of trade," he said.
How to deal with new U.S. genetically modified crops is also likely to be a contentious issue in the new year.

Last summer, American farmers grew small commercial amounts of gene-altered soybeans and corn for the first time ever. Both of these crops are big export items to Europe, and although they were ruled safe by the European Union, a storm of controversy arose over the use of the new products.

To ease concerns, the EU proposed a complicated system of labeling the crops. U.S. officials have repeatedly said such a system would not be practical, and the Agriculture Department is studying the proposal to see if it can be legally challenged.

Finally, the threat of a trade subsidy war between Washington and Europe reared its ugly head this fall when the EU restarted its grain export subsidy programme. The United States quickly warned that Washington is prepared to fight back with its own subsidies if necessary.
At year's end, however, Glickman said that subsidies would used only as a last resort, and said too much attention was being focused on the issue.
"It doesn't dominate our thinking at all," Glickman said.
